Mr. President, the protection of children and youth, which constitute the vast majority of the population of Africa, remains one of the highest priorities within the region and simultaneously encourages countries to enhance cooperation and to develop effective measures to prevent the smuggling of migrants, while ensuring the protection of their rights, including access to justice without any discrimination and non-criminalization in accordance with the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime and its protocol against the smuggling of migrants. Mr. President, the African Group is of the view that the effective application of the UN standards and norms in crime prevention and criminal justice is fundamental in support of fair, humane, and accountable criminal justice systems. The African Group welcomes the adoption of the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime, strengthening international cooperation for combating certain crimes committed by means of information and communications technology systems, and for the sharing of evidence in electronic form in serious crimes and urges or encourages States to consider signing and ratifying the Convention. In addition, the African Group expresses concerns over the continuous challenge posed by crimes that have an impact on the environment, such as wildlife crime, illicit trafficking in precious metals and illegal mining, and illicit trafficking in waste, and commends ongoing efforts to improve effective measures to prevent and counter these crimes. The African Group reiterates that the UNODC needs adequate and sustainable resources to allow it to effectively implement an increasingly complex mandate, including through enhancing the provision of technical assistance and capacity building programs to African countries upon request to enable them to implement their relevant commitments. Therefore, the group urges all states The Group urges all States to increase their unconditional contributions, specifically to the General Purpose Fund of the UNODC, considering the current liquidity crisis that the UN currently finds itself in. Mr. President, the African Group believes that the fight against crime is a common responsibility. While recognizing our shared responsibility to uphold human dignity, human rights, and fundamental freedoms, the African groups calls on the full respect of the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states, their national laws, as well as their social, cultural, and religious peculiarities in full respect for their cultural diversity. The Afghan group wishes us all a successful session. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you very much, Your Excellency. I now give the floor to the representative of the Asia-Pacific Group, Mr. Majed Al-Qatarnah, Ambassador of Jordan to the United Arab Emirates. Your Excellency, the floor is yours.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Asia Pacific Group. The group warmly welcomes the assumption of His Excellency Abdullah bin Sultan Al-Naimi, Minister of Justice of the United Arab Emirates, of the presidency of the General Committee of the 15th United Nations Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice. We extend our full support to you, sir, and to all members of the Bureau as you undertake the important responsibilities ahead. We express our sincere appreciation to the Government of the United Arab Emirates for its generous hospitality and its outstanding efforts in preparing for the hosting of this important Congress. We commend His Excellency Judge Abdurrahman Murad Al-Balushi, Chairperson of the United Arab Emirates National Organizing Committee, and his team for their exemplary work in developing the Abu Dhabi Declaration. We also thank the Secretariat for its dedicated support throughout the preparatory process. Mr. President, this Congress continues to serve as a unique platform that brings together governments, international and non-governmental organizations, and experts from diverse fields. It enables us to exchange views, share experiences, and advance collective efforts to strengthen crime prevention and criminal justice system. The Asia Pacific group underscores the importance of adopting and implementing effective measures to prevent and combat the smuggling of migrants and the trafficking in persons while protecting their lives and human rights, particularly women and accompanied children and adolescents. We highlight the need to address the growing involvement of transnational and national organized criminal groups that profit from these crimes and other offenses, and urge Member States to enhance cooperation to combat these crimes. We further urge Member States to criminalize all forms of child sexual abuse and exploitation, including online child sexual abuse material and its distribution. Strengthening international cooperation, improving data collection, and enhancing the identification of perpetrators and their hotspots linked to these crimes are essential to protecting children and ensuring accountability. Mr. President, the group expresses concern about the rise of violence targeting individuals and communities, both offline and online, based on religion or belief, xenophobia and racism. In this regard, we underline the importance of promoting respect for cultural, religious, ethnic and racial diversity. We call upon all states to undertake appropriate measures in accordance with domestic law and applicable international law to foster a culture of tolerance and mutual respect within societies. The Asia-Pacific Group welcomes the adoption of the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime and encourages states to consider signing and ratifying the convention to support its early entry into force. Strengthening international cooperation in combating crimes committed through information and communications technology systems, such as online scams, ransomware attacks, cyber fraud, and cyber-enabled trafficking in person, is essential in today's rapidly evolving digital landscape. We also emphasize that promoting the rule of law and advancing sustainable development are strongly interrelated and mutually reinforcing with crime prevention and criminal justice. In this regard, we highlight the important role of the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in advancing Goal 16 of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Mr. President, the Group stresses the need to respond to the serious challenges posed by the increasing links among transnational organized crime, terrorism and related illicit activities, in particular drug trafficking, trafficking in persons, corruption, trafficking in firearms, cybercrime, online scams and money laundering. Addressing these challenges requires integrated and multidisciplinary approaches. including reliable data collection, research, and where appropriate, intelligence and analysis sharing, as well as capacity building and technical assistance to support effectively policy making and interventions. Finally, the Asia Pacific Group attaches great importance to the outcome of this Congress and underscores the need for effective and adequate follow-up to the commitment undertaken within its framework. Thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you very much. I now give the floor to the representative of the European Union, His Excellency Karl Halirag, Permanent Representative of the European Union in Vienna. Excellency, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, Ministers, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states, Albania, Armenia, Iceland, Montenegro, Norway, the Republic of North Macedonia, the Republic of Moldova, Serbia, and Ukraine align themselves with this statement. It's an abbreviated version. The full version will be made available online. Mr. President, we would like first to congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election and ensure you and the whole Bureau of our full support. We would also like to thank the United Arab Emirates for hosting the 15th United Nations Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in Abu Dhabi. His Excellency Judge Al-Blushi guided us skillfully through the negotiations of the declaration, which has the full support of the European Union and its Member States and provides a strong basis for our collective action in the years ahead. We are committed to its effective implementation. We also deeply appreciate the excellent work of the Secretariat under the leadership of Executive Director Monica Juma. The European Union remains a strong and reliable partner of UNODC. Mr. President, we meet at a time when armed conflict, geopolitical, environmental and social instability, and attacks on the rules-based international order create unprecedented opportunities for criminal networks. Protecting and supporting victims of all crimes, safeguarding their rights, ensuring equal access to justice for all, and offering the help needed to cope with the damages for all remain non-negotiable pillars of our response. In this context, the recently adopted revision of the EU's Victims' Rights Directive is a powerful tool at our disposal. Mr. President, The European Union and its Member States are deeply alarmed by the scale, brutality and profitability of migrant smuggling. Criminal networks treat human beings as commodities, exploiting vulnerability for immense financial gain with complete disregard for human life and dignity. These networks are closely intertwined with human trafficking, which is both a crime and a human rights violation. The Global Alliance to Counter Migrant Smuggling serves as a vital platform for strengthening international cooperation to dismantle the criminal business model, follow the money, and target those who profit from exploitation, not those who are exploited. We encourage all Member States, international organizations, and partners to join this Global Alliance and actively contribute. Crimes that affect the environment can cause irreversible harm to biodiversity and the environment, human health and livelihoods, while generating massive illicit profits, undermining the rule of law and contributing to instability. In this respect, the Environmental Crime Directive and the Council of Europe Convention on Environmental Crime significantly strengthen our fight against these crimes. A central driver across these criminal ecosystems is drug trafficking. The global drug phenomenon has become increasingly complex, violent, and dynamic, with direct consequences for the safety, security, health, and well-being of society and for international security. As reflected in the EU drug strategy, we address the world drug situation through an evidence-based, integrated, multidisciplinary, and human rights-centered approach. Mr. President, corruption and money laundering are the oxygen on which organized crime depends. Money laundering nourishes criminal groups by protecting criminal proceeds. To prevent and reduce organized crime, we must deprive it of its profits through comprehensive anti-corruption frameworks. Furthermore, we strongly condemn terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. We call for strengthened international cooperation to counter terrorism, address radicalization leading to violent extremism, disrupt terrorist financing, and combat trafficking in firearms, as well as other forms of trafficking that generate proceeds and may be exploited by terrorist or criminal networks, always in full respect of international law, including international human rights law. Mr. President, to counter these threats effectively, we must urgently strengthen international judicial and law enforcement cooperation, while reinforcing the effective implementation of our obligations under the relevant UN conventions, and promote universal ratification of the UN Convention against Cybercrime, while prioritizing already now its implementation. The European Union already works closely with third countries and plans to strengthen the mandates of Eurojust, whose President is with us in this conference, Europol and the European Public Prosecutor's Office to expand their operational relations with their strategic partners. Effective crime prevention, including through holistic, evidence-based strategies that address the root causes and risk factors associated with crime and criminal justice, must be firmly grounded in the rule of law and human rights. Strong, independent, accessible and quality justice systems are the foundation of public trust and resilient societies. This also requires multi-stakeholder partnerships, including with civil society. Criminal networks have repeatedly shown how quickly they can exploit emerging technologies. The European Union is making use of technologies to strengthen its criminal justice response, notably with the new e-evidence framework, which allows access to electronic evidence quickly and efficiently within the EU's borders. While artificial intelligence and digital tools can strengthen justice systems, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms privacy and data protection must be fully safeguarded under clear legal frameworks and meaningful human oversight. Finally, our commitment to human dignity means that the European Union and its Member States strongly oppose the death penalty at all times and in all circumstances as an irrevocable, inhumane and cruel punishment. We call upon all states retaining it to establish a moratorium as a first step towards universal abolition. Mr. President, the challenges before us are global, interconnected and evolving. No state can confront them alone. The European Union and its member states remain committed to strengthening multilateral cooperation to ensure that organized crime finds no safe haven, no impunity and no profit. And now our pledge. As our pledge for justice commitment, the European Union pledges to launch significant new initiatives to counter organized crime and terrorism, such as the forthcoming TEMIS and INTERCEPT projects, designed to strengthen capacity in the criminal justice and anti-trafficking domains, thereby contributing to the implementation of the Abu Dhabi Declaration. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Your Excellency. We will now continue with the national statement. I would kindly ask all the speakers to adhere to the agreed upon speaking time of three to a max of five minutes. Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, It is an honor to speak on behalf of Uzbekistan at a Congress that has spent seven decades trying to make the world a little safer for people who never asked to be afraid. Our thanks to the United Arab Emirates for hosting us in this magnificent city of Abu Dhabi, and to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime for work that rarely makes headlines, but changes lives all the same. Dear delegates, we meet at a difficult moment in human history. Crises are touching one region after another. and crime itself has changed shape. It crosses borders with ease, moves through technology, adapts faster than the system built to contain it. But behind every one of those shifts is something simpler and harder to ignore. A family that felt it directly, a child exploited online, a woman who stayed silent too long, afraid that speaking would cost her more than her silence. A community that had quietly stopped trusting the people meant to protect it. That is the weight we carry into this room, and it is why prevention and justice cannot remain abstract ideas discussed at a distance. They have to reach people or they mean nothing at all. This year, ECOSOC elected Uzbekistan for the first time to the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice for the 2027 to 2029 term. We do not take it this as a praise. We take it as responsibility and as an invitation to keep learning from UNODC's expertise. from the OAC's long experience, from every country in this room that has already faced that we have been starting to face. Nearly everything we have built these past years, we built by asking others first. Let me share briefly what we have tried to give our own people so far, measured not by pride, but by how honestly we can report it. On prevention, we built a digitally integrated public safety system, joining community level policing with artificial intelligence and data analytics. Last year, our AI powered emergency response platform processed over 3.4 million citizen reports. And behind every one of those numbers was a person. who reached out in a moment of need and was answered, rather than left to wonder if anyone was listening at all. Following Uzbekistan's signing of the UN Convention against Cybercrime, we adopted a national cybersecurity strategy for 2026 to 2030 and established a National Coordinating Council for Cybersecurity and Combating Cybercrime. Because the fear people carry now follows them online as much as it does in the street. We tried to give something harder still, safety inside people's own homes, where the law had rarely reached before. In 2023, Uzbekistan became the first country in Central Asia to criminalize domestic violence. We built a network of rehabilitation centers and introduced mandatory protection orders. We said plainly what should never have needed saying in the first place, that violence against women and children has no place and tolerance in our society. On the rule of law, we tried to make corruption not merely punishable, but structurally difficult to commit at all. We gave our anti-corruption agency real independence and introduced real-time monitoring of public procurement. Uzbekistan has risen 34 places on the corruption perception index, a number that matters only because it means fewer people had to pay in some quiet and unfair way for services that should have been theirs by right. In 2027, we will host the 12th session of the Conference of the States Parties to the UN Convention against Corruption, and we hope to arrive at that meeting having learned as much as we bring. And everything above was shaped in partnership, not in isolation. Our national strategy Countering Extremism and Terrorism for 2021-2026 was developed in close consultation with the OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and reinforced through sustained cooperation with UNODC. Excellencies, now I would like to offer something back. Under our Pledge for Justice initiative, Uzbekistan commits to five goals by 2031 on environmental justice, on judicial digitalization, a regional platform for operational and digital cooperation on criminal matters, on transnational security, on counter-narcotics cooperation, and on protecting children in digital spaces. None of this is claimed that we have arrived somewhere others have not. It is an offer to keep working beside this Congress and an honest admission that we still have far more to learn than we have to teach. When we welcome you to Tashkent in 2031, we do not wish to be judged by what in we promised here today. We would rather be judged by something quieter and harder to measure. whether fewer children were harmed, whether fewer women felt that they had to stay silent, and whether fewer families were left to face fear entirely on their own. Thank you.

Kuwait has also attached particular importance to combating cybercrime as part of its efforts to prevent the spread of all forms of transnational crime. In this context, we enacted the law against information technology crimes as the principal national legislative framework We have also supported international efforts to combat the illicit use of ICTs by joining the UN Convention against Cybercrime. We also issued legislation regulating digital commerce in order to establish a comprehensive legal framework governing online commercial transactions and protecting consumer rights. Colleagues, international efforts to prevent and combat crime constitute a shared responsibility among states, implemented through international agreements and national legislation. Three entities have also been established to implement this law, the Financial Intelligence Unit, a National Committee for Combating Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing, comprising all relevant national authorities and working to implement the comprehensive strategy in this regard. and a committee responsible for implementing Security Council resolutions related to counterterrorism and terrorist financing. In closing, I hope that this Congress will contribute to reaching understandings and decisions that strengthen international cooperation in combating and preventing crime and promoting criminal justice.
Thank you very much, Your Excellency. And now we will give--.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, It's a great honor for me to be here today as Minister of Justice of Belgium at a Congress that brings together countries from across the world around the shared responsibility, making our societies safer while in crime prevention and criminal justice. Belgium has consistently supported UNODC's work, including through a recent contribution of 500,000 euro for legal reforms aimed at combating drug trafficking and organized crime in Latin America. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, the challenge before us is clear. Organized criminal networks are increasingly connected, agile, and sophisticated. They operate across borders, exploit new technologies and legitimate infrastructure, infiltrate our economies and target our communities and young people. Our response must evolve accordingly. For Belgium, this means tackling organized crime from every angle, preventing it from taking root disrupting its business model, protecting those it targets, and bringing criminals to justice. As a major European logistic hub, Belgium has witnessed how criminal networks exploit legitimate supply chains, particularly for drug trafficking. Their activities generate violence and corruption and undermine public trust. Belgium is therefore strengthening port security, where international cooperation, including within the framework of the IMO, has an important role to play. Within our government, we have also established a task force on organizing crime to tackle the entire criminal chain. But prosecution alone is not enough. We need prevention and early intervention. combined with administrative and judicial action. This is particularly important when criminal networks target young people. We must prevent vulnerable young people from becoming instruments of organized crime. And at the same time, those who deliberately exploit minors for criminal purposes must be held accountable. Belgium has therefore introduced enhanced penalties for offenses involving the use of minors. Excellencies, if we want to dismantle organized crime, we must dismantle its financial foundations. Crime must not pay. Belgium is strengthening its asset-oriented approach to better identify, trace, freeze, confiscate, and recover criminal assets. Building on European initiatives, Belgium is introducing two forms of confiscation without a prior criminal conviction. First, confiscation will be possible where a conviction for the offence that generated the illicit proceeds cannot be obtained, for example, following the death of the offender. And second, we will introduce the confiscation of unexplained wealth linked to criminal activities. In the coming weeks, the Belgian government will submit draft legislation to put these measures into effect. Our objective is simple. Criminal organizations should not be able to hide or retain the proceeds of their activities behind legal or procedural barriers. And when assets are recovered, they should, whenever possible, serve society again. by compensating victims and supporting law enforcement, prevention and the resilience of our societies. At the same time, an effective fight against crime must never come at the expense of the principles we seek to protect. The rule of law, fundamental rights and the rights of victims must remain at the centre of our criminal justice systems. Whether we are dealing with criminal or organized crime, domestic violence, sexual violence against women and children, or other serious offenses, our response must be coordinated and victim-centered. Respect for fundamental rights is not an obstacle to security. It is one of its foundations. Excellencies, no country can address these challenges alone. Criminal networks cooperate across borders every day. They share information, move money and exploit differences between jurisdictions. Our cooperation must therefore be stronger. Belgium therefore supports stronger implementation of the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime. deeper operational cooperation, faster information sharing, stronger frameworks for asset recovery, and more effective extradition procedures. The good bilateral cooperation between Belgium and the United Arab Emirates is a positive example. Belgium also supports, within a coordinated EU framework, the launch of negotiations on an additional protocol to the Convention addressing crimes that affect the environment. These crimes increasingly involve organized networks operating across borders and require a coherent global response. Ultimately, our objective is not simply to respond to crime after it occurs. It is to prevent criminal networks from gaining a foothold, to stop them from exploiting our young people, to deprive them of the profits that fuel their activities, and to protect our institutions, economies, and communities. Let us send a clear message from this Congress: there can be no safe haven for criminal profits, no tolerance for violence and exploitation, and no compromise on justice and the rule of law. Criminals already know how to cooperate across borders. Our cooperation must be stronger. Thank you. And with regard to our pledge, with a view to advance crime prevention and criminal justice, I pledge for Belgium to adopt within the next 12 months a legislation aimed at improving the effectiveness of its criminal justice system, in line with its key goal of structurally disrupting the criminal profits model. This measure will include the establishment of a national specialized prosecutor's office dealing with organized economic and financial crime, as well as the legislation to facilitate confiscation of criminal assets without prior conviction. Thank you so much.

For Malta, access to justice remains central to our efforts. Justice systems must be effective, accessible, and responsive. We are also strengthening child-friendly justice, placing the child's best interest at the heart of proceedings through the adoption of child-sensitive approaches that reduce the risk of further trauma. In fully supporting the model pledges of promoting child-centred, inclusive and responsive justice, As further elaborated in the margins of this Congress, Malta stands firmly behind child-centered justice as an essential pillar of people-centered justice. Strong justice systems must, however, be complemented by robust crime prevention and law enforcement. Malta Justice and Home Affairs authorities work closely together to protect communities, uphold the rule of law and respond to evolving criminal threats. I now give the floor to my colleague, Minister Glen Bettenfield.

Thank you, my colleague, Minister Grima. Dear Excellencies, Malta pursues a whole of government approach to tackling crime, recognising that effective responses depend upon close cooperation between justice and law enforcement authorities. Malta continues to rank among the safest countries in the world. In 2025, reported crime fell by a further 6%, reaching one of the lowest levels recorded in recent decades. These achievements are not accidental. They are the result of our shift in community-oriented, intelligence-led policing, with a strong focus on prevention, public engagement and proactive enforcement. But while our streets have become safer, crime has adapted, presenting new challenges that require us also to continuously adapt. We are also intensifying our response to organised crime, including drug trafficking, financial crime and the criminal networks that exploit new technologies. This requires continued investment in law enforcement capacity. intelligence-led and evidence-based policing, as well as training of law enforcement authorities to address increasingly sophisticated criminal threats. The fight against trafficking in persons and the smuggling of migrants remains a priority for my government. These crimes exploit the most vulnerable, undermine human dignity, and generate substantial profits for organized criminal networks. We remain firmly committed to preventing exploitation, protecting and supporting victims, and raising public awareness through initiatives such as the Blue Heart campaign. We seek to encourage vigilance, reporting, and the protection of victims. We also cooperate closely with our international partners, including UNODC and Interpol, because these criminal networks transcend borders. and therefore require a united international response. Malta firmly believes that resilient and secure societies can only be built on the justice and law enforcement systems that protect the most vulnerable. We are therefore committed to ensuring that no child and no vulnerable person is left without protection. And for this reason, the Malta Police Force continues to invest in child-centered policing, strengthening victim support services, enhance child protection mechanisms, and deepen cooperation between competent authorities to deliver a more victim-focused response. As an island state situated at the crossroads of key maritime routes, Malta is equally conscious of the need to address maritime crime, We remain committed to continue strengthening maritime security, disrupting illicit trafficking networks and promoting coordinated action at sea. Excellencies. As we look ahead, let us be guided by a simple principle: that criminals must never be more agile than the institutions that protect our citizens. The threats we face are evolving, but so too our resolve, our cooperation, and our capacity to respond. Together, we have the tools, the partnership, and the determination to make our society safer, more resilient, and more secure. Let us, therefore, move forward with unity and determination to deliver effective, people-centred solutions that prevent crime, protect the vulnerable and reinforce confidence in our institutions. Malta stands ready to contribute these shared efforts. Thank you.
